extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, MCs, and crowd-work performers (especially newer acts)
extracted.subtask_short: responding to hecklers in stand-up comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for handling heckles during live stand-up and MCing, covering tactics (ask to repeat, repeat the heckle), use of prepared lines, matching severity to the situation, and delivery/persona considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laugh along when a heckle is genuinely funny
rubrics_metrics.description: If a heckler shouts out something genuinely funny and the audience laughs, the best reaction is to laugh along and allow them their 'win'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughing with the audience accepts their joke; if possible, add to their joke to build on it. This prevents unnecessary escalation and keeps the audience onside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat the heckle or ask them to repeat it
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone heckles, it's common practice to repeat it so everyone has heard what you're responding to, or ask them to repeat what they said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposes: buys time to think of a response; exposes the heckler (their line often sounds worse on repeat); engages the audience and creates pressure on the heckler; sometimes they won't repeat, leaving nothing to respond to (you can comment on their lack of commitment). You may repeat it multiple times—the remark weakens each time. Hearing it again gives more material for a comeback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prepared 'ready-made' comebacks as a backup
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a few prepared lines to handle common types of heckles, especially useful for newer comedians to reduce anxiety and avoid freezing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepared lines buy time for spontaneity; knowing you have a fallback frees you to craft original responses. Prepare responses for common heckles (e.g., 'You're shit!', 'Tell us a joke!', 'Get off!'). These are practical fallbacks if nothing wittier occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure prepared lines fit your established persona and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Any prepared line needs to fit the comedian's established persona and comedic style; the same line can fall flat if it doesn't feel authentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dry, sarcastic comic will deliver lines differently than an energetic observational comic. Authenticity matters: tailor lines to your voice and practice delivery so they feel natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery is crucial: confidence, timing, and eye contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Even brilliant prepared lines will fail if delivered poorly; the comedian must convey control, not flustered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key elements: confidence, timing, and eye contact. Good delivery signals you're in control and makes put-downs land. Practice these skills as much as writing the lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the severity of your put-down to the interruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-set put-downs come in categories and must mirror the 'severity' of what has been said; use milder lines for small interruptions and stronger lines for more aggressive heckles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misreading the mood by using a full-on strong put-down for a minor whisper or small interruption will damage rapport. Continuously 'read the room' to pick appropriate severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve the strongest put-downs as a last resort for persistent hecklers
rubrics_metrics.description: If someone heckles repeatedly throughout the show, then a 'last resort' strong put-down is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the strongest lines only when necessary; examples provided include explicit strong lines (noted in the text). Understand the impact: these lines have real force and should be used sparingly and deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: It's acceptable to use commonly shared professional put-downs
rubrics_metrics.description: There are about thirty shared pre-prepared put-downs that most professional comics typically use; unlike material, it is not considered stealing to use a set put-down many comics know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using shared lines is standard practice. However, you should still choose lines appropriate to the situation and your persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop bespoke put-downs tied to your personal identity/persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing your own prepared put-downs using references to your appearance, age, sex, sexuality, race, religion, philosophy, etc., makes them more authentic and specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bespoke lines that reflect your persona can be more effective than generic ones. Many comics build a small set of personal put-downs and use them over years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose or defuse clumsy or disruptive heckles rather than escalate
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning to disruptive heckles that aren't witty, the aim is often to expose the heckler or defuse the interruption instead of escalating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include asking for repetition (which often weakens the heckle), commenting on lack of commitment ('I must be hearing things'), or using a mild put-down suited to the disruption. Avoid overreacting to minor comments to prevent spoiling the room's mood.
